```{r}
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_bw())
library(dplyr)
library(vroom)
```

```{r}
data("diamonds")
```

# Introduction to `filter`

## Link between diamond carat and price

```{r}
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_point()
```

## Selecting a subset of a dataset

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds_2ct <- diamonds |>
  filter(abs(carat - 2) <= 0.1)
```

```{r}
ggplot(diamonds_2ct, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_point()
```

```{r}
nb_diamonds_near_2 <- diamonds_2ct |> nrow()
nb_diamonds_below_2 <- diamonds_2ct |>
  filter(carat < 2) |> 
  nrow()
```

## Gap in the distribution

There are:

- `r nb_diamonds_below_2` diamonds with weight between 1.9 and 1.99 carats
- `r nb_diamonds_near_2-nb_diamonds_below_2` diamonds with weight between 2 and 2.1 carats

There is a clear gap in the distribution of the weights, with a very small number of diamonds just before 2 carats compared to the number of them just after 2 carats.

## Prices of 2 carat diamonds

```{r}
diamonds |>
  filter(carat >= 2, carat <= 2.1) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = carat, y = price, group = carat)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

## Prices of 2 carat diamonds

```{r}
diamonds |>
  filter(carat >= 2, carat <= 2.1) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = carat, y = price, group = carat)) +
  geom_violin()
```

## Using filter {.smaller}

Filter is used as follows

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
filter(dataframe, expression with a logical value)
```

Interpretation: the code keeps the rows of the data frame for which the expression evaluates to `TRUE`.

```{r}
filter(diamonds, price == 1000) |>
  ggplot(aes(y=cut)) +
    geom_bar()
```

## Multiple logical expressions {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
Filter can be used as follows

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
filter(dataframe, exp1, exp2, exp3)
```

Interpretation: the code keeps the rows of the data frame for which all expressions evaluate to `TRUE`.
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
filter(diamonds, price == 1000, cut == "Ideal" ) |>
  ggplot(aes(y=color)) +
    geom_bar()
```
:::
:::::

# Logical expressions

## Comparison operators

Everything that compares two values and returns `TRUE` or `FALSE`.

```{r}
#| echo: true
x <- 2
x == 2
x >= 3
```

List: `<`, `<=`, `==`, `>=`, `>` and `!=`

## Logical operators

Combining true value.

```{r}
#| echo: true
TRUE & FALSE
TRUE | FALSE
!FALSE
```

- `|` logical OR
- `&` logical AND
- `!` logical NOT

## Examples

Two equivalent filter operations:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
diamonds |> filter(price == 1000, cut == "Ideal") 
diamonds |> filter( (price == 1000) & (cut == "Ideal") ) 
```

Two different filter operations:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
diamonds |> filter(price == 1000, cut == "Ideal") 
diamonds |> filter( (price == 1000) | (cut == "Ideal") ) 
```

# Introduction to `summarise`

## Global summaries

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |> 
  summarise(mean(price), median(price))
```

`summarise` is used as follows:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
summarise(dataframe, expression based on an aggregation function)
```

The result is a data frame with one column per expression and one row.

## Aggregation functions {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
An aggregation function computes a statistics (in a broad sense) on a numerical vector, for instance

- `mean`
- `median`
- `sd`: standard deviation
- `var`: variance
- `max` and `min`
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
x <- c(-0.1, 1, 2, 2, -3, 5)
mean(x)
median(x)
sd(x)
min(x)
n_distinct(x)
length(x)
```
:::
:::::

## Limitations of `summarise` {.smaller}

Aggregation functions are mostly limited to numerical values (and to logical ones to some extent). Aggregation functions for non numerical vectors generally output multiple values.

```{r}
#| echo: true
y <- c("A", "A", "B", "C", "A", "B", "C", "C", "D")
table(y)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |> 
  pull(cut) |>
  table()
```

This generates an error because the aggregation contains multiple values.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
diamonds |>
  summarise(table(cut))
```

## Renaming the resulting columns

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |> 
  summarise(mean_price = mean(price), 
            median_price = median(price), 
            interquartile_price = IQR(price))
```

In many dplyr verbs, one can give to an expression a name in the form `name=expression`. The name will be used for the corresponding column.

# Grouped operations

## Grouped summaries {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  summarise(median_price = median(price), 
            .by = cut)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Effects of `.by`

1)  split the data frame into as many sub-data frames as values taken by the `.by` variable
2)  apply the aggregation functions to each sub-data frame
3)  glue together the resulting one row data frames
4)  add a column to identify the subsets
:::
:::::

## Manual calculation for one value

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  filter(cut == "Ideal") |>
  summarise(median_price = median(price))
```

## Graphical investigation

```{r}
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x=price, colour = cut)) +
  geom_density(bw="sj", linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.75)
```

## Additional statistics

Statistics summarising the price distribution given the cut.

```{r}
diamonds |>
  summarise(median = median(price), 
            mean = mean(price),
            sd = sd(price),
            IQR = IQR(price),
            .by = cut) |>
  arrange(cut)
```

## Counting stuff

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |> 
  summarise(count = n(), 
            .by = cut)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |> 
  group_by(cut) |> 
  summarise(count = n())
```
:::
:::::

## Dependencies

A standard way to assess dependency between two numerical variables is Pearson's correlation coefficient: `cor`.

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
diamonds |>
  summarise(cor(carat, price))
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
diamonds |>
  summarise(cor(carat, price), .by=cut)
```
:::
:::::

## Dependencies (non numerical) {.smaller}

```{r}
diamonds |>
  ggplot(aes(x=cut, fill=color)) +
  geom_bar(position="stack")
```

## Dependencies (non numerical)

```{r}
diamonds |>
  summarise(n(), .by=c(cut, color)) |>
  slice(1:5) ## first five rows
```

# Operating on columns

## Introduction to `mutate`

The `mutate` verb is used to create new columns (or to modify existing ones) based on calculation conducted on existing columns. Generic form:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
mutate(dataframe, newcolumn = expression)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds_ppc <- diamonds |>
  mutate("price per carat" = price/carat)
```

## Application example

```{r}
diamonds_ppc |>
  summarise(median(`price per carat`), .by=cut) |>
  arrange(cut)
```

## Application example (graphical)

```{r}
diamonds_ppc |>
  ggplot(aes(x=`price per carat`, colour = cut)) +
  geom_density(bw="sj", linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.75)
```

## Grouped mutate

```{r}
diamonds_ppc |>
  summarise(median = median(`price per carat`), 
            mean = mean(`price per carat`),
            sd = sd(`price per carat`),
            IQR = IQR(`price per carat`),
            .by = cut) |>
  arrange(cut)
```

## Global extreme diamonds

We want to study "extreme diamonds" in terms of price per carat.

```{r}
diamonds_ppc |>
  filter(`price per carat` > 10000) |>
  slice(1:5) |>
  select(1:6)
```

## Global extreme diamonds (graphics)

This selects diamonds with a price (per carat) larger than the average one + 2 times its standard deviation.

```{r}
diamonds_ppc |>
  filter(`price per carat` > mean(`price per carat`) + 2 * sd(`price per carat`)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=`price per carat`, colour = cut)) +
  geom_density(bw="sj", linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_rug(alpha = 0.5)
```

```{r}
diamonds_with_stats <- 
  diamonds_ppc |>
    mutate(mean = mean(`price per carat`), 
           sd = sd(`price per carat`), 
           large_ppc = mean + 2*sd)
```

## Conditional analysis.

```{r}
diamonds_with_cond_stats <- 
  diamonds_ppc |>
    mutate(mean = mean(`price per carat`), 
           sd = sd(`price per carat`), 
           large_ppc = mean + 2*sd,
           .by = cut)
```

```{r}
diamonds_with_cond_stats |>
  filter(`price per carat` > large_ppc) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=`price per carat`, colour = cut)) +
  geom_density(bw="sj", linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_rug(alpha = 0.5)
```

# Application to discrete data

## Visual conditional distributions

```{r}
diamonds |>
  ggplot(aes(x=cut, fill=color)) +
  geom_bar(position="fill")
```

## Conditional frequencies {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds_counts <- 
  diamonds |>
    summarise(n(), 
              .by=c(cut, color)) 
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds_cond_counts <-
  diamonds_counts |> 
  mutate(freq = `n()`/sum(`n()`), 
         .by=cut)
```
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
diamonds_cond_counts |>
  slice(1:5)
```
:::
:::::

# Slice

## Slice principle {.smaller}

`filter` subsets rows based on some conditions on the values inside cells. 
`slice` and friends do the same but based on the positions of the rows. 

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  slice(2:6)
```

## Slice variations {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  slice(1, .by = cut)
```

## Max and min {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  slice_min(price)
```
```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  slice_min(price, with_ties = FALSE)
```

## Grouped max/min {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  slice_max(carat, by = cut)
```

## Other slice functions {.smaller}

- `slice_head`: selects rows from the top of the data frame
- `slice_tail`: selects rows from the bottom of the data frame
- `slice_sample`: selects a random sample of the rows (uniform distribution without replacement by default)

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  slice_sample(by=cut, weight_by = price/carat)
```

# Select

## Select principle

The goal of the function is to select some of the variables in a data frame, based on 
the properties (position, name and content).

The basic use leverages names:

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  slice_tail(n=5) |>
  select(price, carat, cut)
```

## Select with position

Select can use columns indexes in a similar way to `slice`.

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  slice_max(carat, by = color) |>
  select(1:4, 7)
```

## Select by column name properties

Select can operate by looking at conditions on the names.

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  slice_max(carat, n = 5) |>
  select(starts_with("c"))
```

```{r}
#| message: false
credit_default <- vroom(here("data", "default-of-credit-card-clients.csv"))
```

## Select by column name properties

```{r}
#| echo: true
credit_default |>
  slice_max(LIMIT_BAL) |>
  select(starts_with("PAY_")) |>
  select(1:6)
```
## Select by column name properties

```{r}
#| echo: true
credit_default |>
  slice_max(LIMIT_BAL) |>
  select(matches("PAY_[0-9]"))
```
## Select by column content properties 

Select can test the content of a column using a specified function. 

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  slice_sample(n=5) |>
  select(where(is.numeric))
```

## Select by column content properties 

Select can test the content of a column using a specified function. 

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  slice_sample(n=5) |>
  select(where(is.factor))
```

## Combination of selections

Selection formulae can be combined using the standard logical operators 
`|`, `&` and `!`.

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  slice_sample(n=5) |>
  select(price | where(is.factor))
```

## Combination of selections

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  slice_sample(n=5) |>
  select(!starts_with("c"))
```

# Sorting

## arrange

The `arrange` verb is used to sort a data frame according to various properties.

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  summarise(median(carat), .by=clarity) |>
  arrange(clarity) # increasing order of clarity
```

## Using calculated column

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  summarise(median(carat), .by=clarity) |>
  arrange(`median(carat)`)
```

## Decreasing order

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  summarise(n = n(), .by = color) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

## Lexicographic order {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true
diamonds |>
  summarise(n = n(), .by = c(cut, color)) |>
  arrange(cut, desc(color)) |>
  slice(1:8)
```

# Tidyr main operations

```{r}
library(tidyr)
```


## Tidy data

Data set with important properties:

1)  each row is a statistical unit (a person)
2)  each column is a property of statistical units (the weight in kg of person)
3)  each type of statistical unit is described by a single table (or data frame)

Implicit point: each cell contains a single value

## Ambiguous situations

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
diamonds_counts |>
  slice(1:8)
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Is (Ideal, E, 3903) the description of a statistical unit wrt some variables? 

- this is a group of diamonds
  - cut
  - colour
  - size of the group
- changing the precision of the analysis

:::
:::::

## Tidyr functionalities

1) pivoting from wide to long and vice versa
   a) untidy representation of tidy data can be very usefull
   b) moving from tidy to untidy and back again is quite common
2) spliting the content of a cell

## Untidying for readability

```{r}
diamonds_counts |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = color, names_from = cut, values_from = `n()`)
```

## Pivot wider principles

- `id_cols`: identified the statistical unit, one per unique value in the column(s)
- `names_from`: the column that contains the names of the characteristics of the statistical units
- `values_from`: the column that contains the values of the characteristics of the statistical units

Generic example: (id1, id2, ..., idn, name, value)

```{r}
#| message: false
le_who_raw <- vroom(here("data","life expectancy raw.csv"))
```

## Who example {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true
le_who_raw |> 
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(Location, Period),
              names_from = c(Indicator, Dim1),
              values_from = Value) |>
  select(Location, Period,  `Life expectancy at birth (years)_Male`) |>
  slice_min(`Life expectancy at birth (years)_Male`, n = 5)
```
## Who example {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true
le_who_raw |> 
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(Location, Period),
              names_from = c(Indicator, Dim1),
              values_from = Value) |>
  filter(Location == "France") |>
  ggplot(aes(x=Period, y=`Life expectancy at birth (years)_Female`)) +
  geom_line()
```
